transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Hollowmoot [L-03].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the plank streets of Hollowmoot, and the market stalls have gone quiet under grey sheets of water. A woman named Sela wades through the crowd barefoot, her shawl soaked black, and seizes whichever of you looks least likely to turn her away. "My boy—Tomas—he heard it three nights past, the singing from the belltower. He walked right into the flood after it and I couldn't stop him." Behind her, up on the stilted watchtower, the quarantine bell begins its slow iron toll, and heads turn all along the causeway rail. Somewhere in the crowd, a Warden starts pushing through toward the commotion, hand on the hilt of a torch-iron.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear it. Step aside—I can help her son in ways you can't.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps directly into the Warden's path, planting herself between him and Sela. She straightens to her full height, rain streaming down her face, speaking with absolute certainty like this is her responsibility to claim. "I hear the song too, Warden. That boy walked toward the bells, and that's my burden to handle, not yours.")

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I'm an exorcist, Sela—I hunt the things that call with voices not their own. Tell me exactly what your son heard from that belltower. Every word of the song, if he repeated any of it to you.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (I step forward with clear authority, placing myself between Sela and the approaching Warden, my bearing steady and practiced. My attention is entirely on the grieving mother now—cataloging her details, listening for the precision in her words. The mention of a singing bell in this marshland means something specific, and I need the truth before the quarantine bell's ringing brings authority down on all of us.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Tell me everything, quickly—when did Tomas wander, and how long ago? I've seen the hive-touch before, and we're not losing him to a bell and a Warden's torch.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock firmly takes Sela's arm, her weathered hands steady. She plants herself between the mother and the approaching Warden, eyes fixed on Sela with the unshakeable certainty of someone who's delivered babies in floods and fire alike. There's no hesitation in her stance, no doubt—only the professional focus of a midwife who knows what needs doing.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Tomas heard the singing from the belltower—the same song everyone's been hearing—and it pulled him into the flood. That's the Hive Blight calling. Tell me everything, Sela. I need to know.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow places a steady hand on Sela's shoulder, anchoring her to the moment. He turns to face the approaching Warden with the calm assurance of someone who once wore the uniform himself, placing himself between the officer and the grieving mother.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Warden Corvin. I remember the oath, and I remember why I broke it—because some things matter more than the watch's chains. I'm not running from that debt today. I'm standing it.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Rapport: dice 0 - 0 +, invoking Bell-Ringer's Apprentice Who Hears the Swarm-Song [PE-HC] → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's voice cuts through the rain with a certainty that makes even Warden Corvin pause mid-stride. "I hear the song too, Warden" lands like a bell-note of its own — heads turn, and for a moment the crowd sees not a suspect but a bell-ringer claiming a bell-ringer's duty. Corvin's hand eases off the torch-iron; whatever quarrel he came to pick, it isn't worth picking with a girl who speaks the swarm's language back at it. Sela sags into Caddock's grip, words tumbling out now that no one's dragging her away: three nights of singing, growing louder, Tomas rising from his pallet with his eyes gone glassy and his mouth moving along with a tune he'd never heard before, then gone into the black water before she could catch his sleeve — no words repeated, only the melody, over and over, the same seven notes Anselm has heard described before in older, drier books. Yarrow's old oath hangs in the air between him and Corvin, unspoken but not forgotten; the Warden's jaw tightens, filing it away rather than forgiving it. The bell up on the watchtower keeps tolling — quarantine, not alarm, but close enough that the crowd is already giving the party a wide, wary berth. By the time the last echo fades, the four of you have effectively claimed Tomas's disappearance as your own business, and no one in Hollowmoot is inclined to argue.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Warden Corvin lets you pass the watchtower chain with a warning rattle of his torch-iron — "Past the pilings, you're the Order's problem, not mine" — and the plank road gives way to black water and leaning reeds. Sela's directions hold true for a while: broken pilings mark an old pilgrim's path, half-swallowed, and the rain needles down cold on the back of your necks. Somewhere ahead, past the drowned rooftops, a bell tolls once, off-rhythm, as if struck by something that isn't a bellringer. The reed mats underfoot look solid enough — but the Mere has swallowed careless feet before, and the temple's not going to give up its dead easily.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: That bell's struck wrong. Something's *calling* it, and I need to see what's doing this.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra pushes forward over the reed mats toward the tolling bell, rain-soaked and intent. She moves fast—not reckless, but certain of her purpose. The swarm-song hums at the edge of her hearing beneath the rain, and the off-rhythm bell-toll makes her bones itch. She traces the sound forward, closing the distance to whatever's striking the bell.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Hold—listen to that bell. Something's striking it without skill, without reverence. That's no bellringer at the tongue.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm raises a fist to stop the group's forward advance and stands motionless on the reed mat, his head tilted toward the temple. He listens to the off-rhythm tolling with the concentration of a man who has spent years learning the language of bells and wards. His jaw tightens—the look of someone remembering old lessons about what happens when something silences a bell's proper song and strikes it blind.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: The reeds hold if you know where to step. Stay to my path, and mind the water—the Mere's hungry, but I know how to feed it lies.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock takes the lead without hesitation, her weathered feet finding purchase on the reed mats with practiced certainty. She reads the water's subtle movements, testing each step before the others follow, her strong frame cutting a path through the marsh. Her fingers trail across the reeds, feeling for the firmest ground—this is her domain, and she moves like she belongs to it.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Stay close to my footfalls, and watch the reeds—the Mere takes the careless.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow moves to the front of the group, his weathered eyes scanning the reed mats for the subtlest shifts in color and texture that mark solid footing versus drowning mud. This is his marsh; he knows where the ground holds and where it gives. His hand rests on Brack's neck, drawing comfort from the marsh hound's solid presence, and he picks out a careful path toward the off-rhythm tolling ahead, alert for the dangers that Sela's desperation might blind her to.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: "My name—it's calling my name—I can't move!"

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice + 0 - -, invoking Bell-Ringer's Apprentice Who Hears the Swarm-Song [PE-HC] → Superb (+5) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — overcome with Physique: dice + - + - → Great (+4) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's dread breaks like a fever—she names the thing calling her name right back, snarling it into the rain, and her own voice steadies her feet. She surges forward with a bell-ringer's certainty, and the swarm-song recoils from her defiance, giving her a clean bearing straight toward the belltower. Caddock reads the mire like a midwife reads a labor, finding the old pilings buried under the reed mats and stamping out a path so sure that even Brack trots it without a stumble. In moments the party is across the worst of the Sucking Mire, boots planted on solid stone steps, the drowned nave of Saint Orrin's rising black and dripping before you—windows shattered, water lapping the altar, and above it all, the belltower where the off-rhythm bell tolls again, closer now, and wrong.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Ring it again! I want to know what you are—and whether you can ring worth a damn!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra charges into the flooded temple without hesitation, splashing across the drowned nave toward the bell-tower stairs. She takes them hard and fast, two at a time, her scarred hands gripping wet stone rails, boots finding purchase on treacherous steps. The off-rhythm tolling hammers louder with each flight—something wrong is ringing *her* bell, and she's going to answer it face-to-face.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The swarm has the bell. I can feel it in the ringing—that's not a bellringer's touch, that's the Hive itself, drawing others to its call through the bell-tongue. This is how the Blight spreads: through voices and songs, through things that should call us to salvation.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm moves to the temple threshold with measured steps, his gaze fixed on the belltower above. He stands perfectly still, listening to the off-rhythm tolling not with his ears alone but with the deeper senses of an exorcist trained to read spiritual corruption. His lips move silently through old wards as his fingers trace invisible runes—the old protections his order taught him. The bell strikes wrong, and he understands: the Hive has claimed the bell-tongue, made it an instrument of the swarm-song's endless call.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Tomas, I'm here—call out! I'm coming for you, boy. The Mere doesn't take anyone on my watch.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock strides into the drowned temple without hesitation, her strong frame moving with practiced confidence through rain-soaked water and crumbling stone. She heads straight for the belltower where the off-rhythm bell tolls, calling out for Tomas in her commanding midwife's voice that cuts through the dissonance.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: There's something in that tower, and it's not a man with a rope. The bell's being called, not rung. We go in careful, or not at all.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow's eyes narrow as he studies the belltower's dark windows, his weathered gaze picking through shadows like a man reading water. Brack whines low and presses against his leg, hackles raised—the hound senses what his bond-brother sees. Something moves in that tower, and it moves wrong. Yarrow steps forward and positions himself between the group and the temple entrance, his hand resting on Brack's neck.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Tomas! Boy, answer me—I didn't cross the Mere in black rain to find you cold! I'm here, and I'm bringing you out of that tower alive, you hear me?

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Athletics: dice + + - - → Good (+3) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — create advantage with Lore: dice - + 0 0 → Great (+4) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — overcome with Physique: dice 0 - 0 -, invoking Swamp Midwife Who Delivers in Any Weather [CA-HC] → Great (+4) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — overcome with Notice: dice + 0 + 0 → Fantastic (+6) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The party crosses the drowned nave together now, all four bound by the same certainty. Petra hits the belltower stairs at a dead run, her boots finding every dry stone Caddock's steady voice seems to summon underfoot—Tomas's name rings out over the water, commanding and unafraid. Anselm doesn't move, but his stillness does more than any charge: he reads the bell's wrongness down to its bones, marking exactly how the Hive has bent the bell-tongue to its purpose, and what it would take to break that grip (Reading the Hive's Touch on the Bell). Yarrow sees it first through the shattered window-slats—a shape up in the dark that is not a boy pulling a rope, limbs too many, too wrong, working the bell like a puppet on strings of sinew. Brack's hackles never go down. By the time the off-rhythm toll sounds a fourth time, the party stands at the base of the belltower stairs, soaked, united, and staring up into a darkness that answers to something other than God.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The belltower stairs open onto a ruined loft where the great bronze bell hangs cracked and silent, wrapped in wet strands of pale, pulsing hive-matter like veins around an old heart. Tomas crouches beneath it, rocking, his eyes fixed upward at nothing — and above him, in the shadows of the rafters, something vast shifts and resettles, patient, listening, its many small voices sighing out in one low chord that isn't quite words. The swarm-song swells louder here than anywhere else in the Sallowmere, pressing at the edges of every skull in the room. Rain sluices through gaps in the roof, and the floor groans under the added weight of four more living bodies.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear you—and you hear ME. Get off him!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra plants her feet on the wet stone and throws her voice at the vast shadow in the rafters—not screaming, but commanding, a bell-ringer's authority cutting through the swarm-song like bronze through fog. Her defiance rings clear and certain.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Tomas. Can you hear me beneath the singing? Tell me—is this a soul that hungers, or merely hunger that's learned to wear a shape?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm stands motionless at the top of the belltower stairs, his exorcist's stillness a counterweight to the swarm-song's press. He studies the vast, patient thing in the rafters and the pale hive-matter pulsing around the bronze bell—watching for intention, for hunger, for anything like will. His hand rests on the iron holy-symbol at his chest, but he doesn't yet move to invoke it.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Tomas—your mother's waiting. Come back to yourself now.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock strides through the filthy water toward Tomas, boots finding solid purchase in the flooded loft even as the swarm-song claws at her ears. She reaches down with both hands—not rough, but with the absolute certainty of someone who's caught drowning mothers and slippery newborns—and grabs him by the shoulders to pull him back from beneath the pulsing hive-matter wrapped around the bell.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Stay behind me—all of you. Whatever's up there in the dark, I'm holding this line.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow strides forward and plants himself between his companions and the shadows above, crossbow raised and ready. His feet settle into the wide, solid stance of someone who's held watch through worse than this—or so he makes it look. He won't let that thing get past him to Tomas or the others.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—I—

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — attack with Rapport: dice + 0 + 0, invoking Bell-Ringer's Apprentice Who Hears the Swarm-Song [PE-HC] → Epic (+7) vs Superb (+5): SUCCESS (The Hive Mother stress 2)

transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Athletics: dice - 0 + - → Fair (+2) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: The Hive Mother attacks Petra (mental): Superb (+5) vs Petra's Will Good (+3) — hit for 2

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's cry lands like a struck bell—the vast shape in the rafters recoils, hive-matter sloughing wet strands into the water below as pain (real pain) ripples through whatever passes for its body. In the same breath Caddock's hands close on Tomas's shoulders and she hauls him bodily away from beneath the bell, clean and certain, stone finding her feet at every step until the boy is sobbing and coughing but free. Yarrow's crossbow-braced stance holds the line true, his wide-planted boots and iron nerve anchoring the loft's narrow footing so nothing gets past him to the others. But the Hive Mother isn't done—she claws back with Petra's own name, a chorus of small drowned voices screaming it in unison, and the assault crashes into Petra like floodwater; she reels, jaw clenched, forcing her knees to lock and her feet to stay planted even as her vision swims and her skull rings with borrowed voices. She's hurt, and the swarm-song hasn't stopped singing her name—but she's still standing, still between Tomas and the dark.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: My name is MINE!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Sweat-cold and reeling, Petra's jaw tightens against the screaming in her skull. She plants her feet and leans into the storm of borrowed voices, hurling her own voice back at the Hive Mother—not screaming, but ringing her name like a struck bell, a bell-ringer's command that demands to be HEARD.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The bell wasn't broken—it was corrupted. The hive uses Saint Orrin's own instrument to call. Silence the bell properly, and we cut this creature's voice.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm moves deeper into the loft, his exorcist's eye reading the pale hive-matter wound around the bronze bell. It's not separate from the creature—it's part of it, a corruption of Saint Orrin's instrument turned into a conduit for the swarm-song. He traces the connection between the entity's movements and the bell's thrumming pulse, understanding now that they are one thing.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: You want him? Come through me first.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock plants herself as a solid barrier between Tomas and the creature, boots finding stone that holds firm even in the flooded loft. She drives forward with the relentless strength of someone who's pulled drowning mothers from the current—her hands, still wet with the effort of hauling Tomas free, reach up toward the pulsing hive-matter as if to tear it away from the bell itself.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Not on my watch.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow swings his crossbow up toward the rafters and fires at the shadow, the bolt cutting toward where the Hive Mother writhes. His stance stays planted firm and wide—a wall between it and Petra—and he won't yield an inch.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Anselm gets his advantage — he traces the corruption and understands the bell as a conduit — but doing it means pressing his bare hand into the pulsing hive-matter itself. A strand splits under his fingers, wet and warm, and a thin line of his own blood mixes with the pale ichor before he wrenches free.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's second cry finishes what the first started—she rings the Hive Mother's own stolen voices back at her until the vast shape convulses, its many small voices fracturing into a single dying wail. Caddock doesn't wait for it to recover: she drives her hands up into the pulsing hive-matter wound around the bell and tears, ripping the creature loose from its ancient anchor even as Yarrow's crossbow bolt punches home dead center. The Hive Mother comes apart—not with a roar, but a long, guttering sigh, pale strands sloughing off the bronze bell and dropping into the black water below, twitching once, then still. The swarm-song cuts out mid-note, and for the first time in eleven years the belltower is silent except for rain and Tomas's ragged sobbing in Caddock's arms. Anselm straightens from where he crouched by the corrupted bell, his palm split and bleeding where the hive-matter caught him—he understands now, with cold certainty, exactly how the bell became a mouth for the thing in the rafters, but that understanding cost him a line of his own blood mixed into the ichor, and he can't yet be sure what that mixing has done. Tomas is alive. The bell is silent. The Hive Mother is dead.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Caddock's hands come away wet and shaking, strands of hive-matter still clinging to her fingers as the vast shape she tore loose convulses against the rafters, its many stolen voices dying into a single wet shriek. The impact sends a shudder through the whole tower — old stone grinding against older stone, water sheeting down through cracks that weren't there a breath ago. Tomas is limp but breathing in Caddock's other arm, and somewhere below the floor groans like it's deciding whether to hold. The cracked bell itself sways on its rotten yoke, hive-matter sloughing off it in ropes, and for the first time in eleven years the swarm-song is silent — but the temple sounds like it's about to answer for that silence.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear it—the tower's voice in the falling stone. This way, and move! Trust the eastern wall, the pilings hold!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra closes her eyes for a single steadying breath as the stone shudders around her. Where the chaos screams, she hears precision—the death-song of the tower written in groaning wood and splitting stone, a language a bell-ringer learns like a second heartbeat. Her eyes open with absolute certainty and she points, moving forward with the same defiant poise she used to face down the swarm-song itself, calling out the safe route through the ruin for anyone behind her.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The conduit's severed. The tower won't hold. To the stairs—now.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm moves with the certain rhythm of someone who has escaped a drowning temple before. He traces the spreading cracks, reads the weight shifting in the old stone, and steers toward the belltower stairs with absolute conviction. His hand bleeds where the hive-matter marked him, but he ignores it—there is no time for wounds when the whole tower is failing.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I've read the worst the swamp can throw at us—stone falls the same way water moves. Move with me, all of you, and nobody stays behind.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock reads the tower's groans like she reads a laboring body's contractions—something honed across years of moving through monsoon and mire. She doesn't hesitate. She shifts Tomas's limp weight to her stronger arm and moves toward the stairs with absolute certainty, her free hand finding every stable stone as the structure shudders around them. She calls out the path without looking back: landing, stairs, the old pilings below, open water beyond. Her hands shake with hive-matter still clinging to her fingers, but her feet are steady and her voice doesn't waver.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: East stairs, now! Don't look at the bell—it's the pillar that matters, and that pillar holds.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow's eyes scan the crumbling tower with the precision of a militia guard who's held impossible positions. He reads the fractures in the stone, traces where the weight is failing first, and spots the east pillar—solid, still standing. He plants himself in the doorway and points with the absolute certainty of someone who's held a line before. "East stairs! That pillar won't fall—move now!")

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—no, that's not—Mom?

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: No time. Watch your footing on those stairs—the corruption spreads quick, but the stone fails faster.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The shrieking wail claws through Caddock's skull—she staggers, teeth gritted, and takes the hit in stride, refusing to let go of Tomas even as her vision swims white at the edges. But Petra's called route holds true: the eastern wall doesn't so much as groan as the party pours down it, stone finding their feet exactly where she promised. Anselm reaches the stairs first, blood-marked hand trailing against the rail, steering by instinct honed in another drowning building years ago. Behind them the belltower gives one last convulsive shudder—the cracked bell tearing free of its rotten yoke and crashing down into black water with a sound like a dying god's last word—and then the swarm-song's silence holds. No new cry rises to replace it. The party spills out onto the temple's half-flooded nave, soaked, shaking, alive, with Tomas breathing ragged but breathing in Caddock's arms. Behind you, Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple settles into a stillness it hasn't known in eleven years.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Stone grinds on stone above you as the belltower's death-shudder rolls down through the temple's bones — the nave floor is already sheeting with new water, old pillars leaning where they shouldn't. Wading toward the broken doors and open sky, you find them blocked: dozens of soaked pilgrims kneel chest-deep in the flood, candles somehow still lit, and at their head stands a gaunt man in sodden priest's vestments, arms spread wide toward the dying wail still echoing in the rafters. "You've silenced Her voice," the Drowned Priest says, almost gentle, almost grieving, "so now you'll drown here with the rest of Her faithful." Behind you, the ceiling groans a warning that won't repeat twice.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear what you hear, priest—but she's silent now. These people walk out of here with me, not down with you. Stand aside or I'll move you myself.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra advances through the rising water, her presence alone cutting through the priest's grief like a bell cutting fog. She reaches toward the kneeling pilgrims with the authority of someone who has already heard the swarm-song and refused to break, her eyes locked on the Drowned Priest as if daring him to test whether a bell-ringer's will might bend stronger than a drowning man's conviction.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Step aside. She's gone. These people aren't faithful—they're drowning. And you're drowning with them because you believed in a lie.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm doesn't look back at the groaning ceiling. He steps forward with the bearing of an exorcist who has traced corruption to its source, who has felt the hive-matter split wet between his fingers and learned its nature intimately. One hand is marked with his own blood mixed with pale ichor. He fixes the Drowned Priest with a gaze that strips away delusion: without the swarm-song, without Her voice calling through open wounds, you are only a man grieving a god that is dead. There is no power holding these pilgrims down anymore but fear and sickness. He speaks with the terrible certainty of one who knows possession when he sees it.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: The tower's falling, priest. Move or drown—I've no time for theology and neither does the stone.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock shifts Tomas's weight and strides forward through the kneeling pilgrims without breaking rhythm, shoulders broad and deliberate. She doesn't go around them—she goes through, steady and inevitable as the tide, while stone grinds against stone above and dust shakes from the rafters.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Through the doors! I'm holding—go NOW!

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow plants himself in the collapsing nave, feet braced wide in the water, arms spread against the groaning stone descending toward them. He locks every muscle with the kind of conviction you learn in militia watches—back straight, jaw set, the immovable presence of someone who will not break his line. It won't stop the collapse. But it'll buy the seconds everyone needs.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The priest's voice finds me like a knife between ribs—he *knows*. I feel the promise like iron in my chest, and for one breath I want to drop my arms, to bargain, to finally learn. But I've got no answers to trade that matter more than getting them out alive.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's words land like a struck bell against the Drowned Priest's chest — he staggers back a step, grief cracking into something rawer, and for the first time the pilgrims' eyes waver toward the doors instead of the rafters. Anselm presses the advantage, naming the lie plainly: without Her voice, there is nothing holding them under but fear — and one by one, hands unclasp, knees rise from the flood. Caddock doesn't wait to see if the words take — she drives through the loosening crowd with Tomas braced against her shoulder, parting soaked robes and candle-smoke like she's done it a hundred times at a bedside, and behind her the pilgrims part clean, no fight left in them. Yarrow plants himself against the collapsing nave, arms spread, the picture of a man who will not move — and when the Drowned Priest turns on him with the promise he made in anger twisting like a blade, Yarrow's jaw only sets harder; he holds, feet locked, the ceiling's groan the only answer he needs. With the crowd broken open and the priest reeling, the party surges past him and out through the temple doors into daylight and rain, just as the nave gives way behind them in a roar of falling stone and black water — Tomas coughing, alive, cradled safe in Caddock's arms.

free_text.best_moment: When Petra screamed her own name back at the Hive Mother in S3. It was the climax of her character arc: a bell-ringer who hears what others can't, refusing to freeze even when called by her own stolen voices, standing between danger and the people she's sworn to protect. She wasn't defending—she was ringing truth into the darkness.
free_text.most_frustrating: The "Mom?" moment in S4 felt like the GM was hinting at something crucial in Petra's past, but it got swept under the temple collapse. I got a taste of a deeper story and wanted to know what that was.
free_text.background_used: Well, with caveats. My bell-ringer senses and my vow to ring everyone home were absolutely central and felt organic to every scene. The compel of my trouble (Freezes When the Song Calls Her Name) was used appropriately. But two aspects—Marked Enemy of the Dry Saint and Raised at Ashwater Tollgate—never surfaced at all. Not sure if they're setup for later or if I should rethink them.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to understand why the swarm-song knew Petra's name specifically and targeted her. That "Mom?" moment felt like it was pointing to something personal in her history, but the session ended before I could follow that thread.
free_text.one_sentence: My core concept was brilliant and central to everything, and my vow made the rescue feel personal, but some character elements sit dormant and mysterious hints about my past feel like they're leading somewhere I haven't reached yet.

free_text.best_moment: Pressing my bare hand into the hive-matter wrapped around the bell to understand how the creature had corrupted it. That moment crystallized what Anselm IS—an exorcist willing to get close to corruption for knowledge—and gave me a personal cost (blood mixing with the ichor) that created real, ongoing uncertainty about what that contact means.
free_text.most_frustrating: The escape sequence (S4-S5) where I felt like Anselm was providing expert analysis rather than driving action. Petra and Caddock owned the physical escape; Yarrow held the line. Anselm read obstacles but didn't feel like he *chose* the way out the same way the others did. Also: the blood-mixing creates narrative weight but no clear mechanical hook to explore what it's done to him—intriguing but slightly unresolved.
free_text.background_used: The "Hunting the Silenced Bell-Tongue of Saint Orrin" aspect was directly central to this session—the bell itself WAS his hunt. It landed perfectly, not forced or coincidental but genuinely thematic. The Drowned Mill background was present as context but didn't activate explicitly, which is fine. Blackwater Lieutenant Vex hasn't come up yet.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted more mechanical action-ownership in the escape sequence—more opportunities for Anselm to *drive* the way out rather than analyze it. Also wanted clearer rules texture around the blood-mixing consequence: is it infection? Corruption? A marker? The game left it beautifully mysterious but without a mechanical handle to engage it.
free_text.one_sentence: Anselm's backstory was used very well—his quest was central and the cost felt personal and unresolved—but he functioned more as the expert consultant than as an active hero in the action sequences.

free_text.best_moment: When Caddock got the Legendary result against the Hive Mother and took it out completely—that moment crystallized everything about her character. She's someone who delivers life even in impossible circumstances, and pulverizing that creature with raw midwife's strength felt exactly right.
free_text.most_frustrating: Caddock's trouble "Cannot Admit Fault, Even to Save a Life" never actually created a choice-point or dilemma. A trouble should complicate things; this one just sat there. Also, I started with 3 fate points and ended with 0, which limits the strategic mechanical play I enjoy—I wanted more opportunities to invoke aspects with real resource costs.
free_text.background_used: The swamp midwife background landed really well—reading the Sucking Mire like a labor, calling Tomas out with a midwife's commanding voice, metaphorically "delivering" him to safety. That thread was consistent and good. But "Last of Marrowreed Village" and "Guardian of the Wick Lane Cellars" never came into play, which felt like a disconnect. Also: there's an aspect about being "Bound to Sella, Once Comrade, Now Hive-Touched," but the Sela in the story was just a grieving mother, not that specific history—felt like a missed opportunity to deepen that connection.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to play the strategic resource-management side of Caddock—hoarding fate points, spending them efficiently, arguing for mechanical advantage. The session's rolls fell well in my favor anyway, but I never got to leverage the resource game itself. I also wanted Caddock's trouble to create actual tension between competing goals, not just sit dormant.
free_text.one_sentence: Caddock's core swamp-midwife identity was woven through every choice and moment really effectively, but the deeper background—the burned village, the hive-touched bond, the guardian role—felt disconnected rather than activated.

free_text.best_moment: Standing against the Drowned Priest in the collapsing temple, feeling the old oath twist like a blade but choosing to hold the line for the others anyway. That moment crystallized everything Yarrow is—the guilt of his past, the refusal to abandon people, the willingness to sacrifice answers for lives.
free_text.most_frustrating: In the final escape, Yarrow became mostly a mechanical obstacle to keep the ceiling up. I understood why narratively, but I felt reactive rather than active—my character was functional scenery for the others' escapes rather than making choices of his own.
free_text.background_used: The oath with Warden Corvin and the Drowned Priest's words about "a promise made in anger" hit the trouble aspect like a bell-strike. That was earned and organic, not forced. But "Questing for the True Source of the Flood" didn't get much real estate—we solved a Hive Blight problem, not the underlying mystery Yarrow came to find.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to dig into the mystery of what's actually causing the flood. Yarrow's aspect is about questing for the true source, but the session resolved around an immediate threat (Tomas, the Hive Mother) rather than that broader question. The game didn't make space for pursuing that thread.
free_text.one_sentence: My disgraced past and role as a line-holder were perfectly used; the quest for the flood's source stayed in the background where it probably belongs until later, but I'd like to see it come forward soon.

chronicle.summary: In Hollowmoot's flooded temple, the party answered a mother's plea and climbed into the belltower to face the Hive Mother herself — Petra's bell-voice broke the swarm-song's grip, Caddock tore the creature loose with her bare hands, and Anselm read its corruption in his own blood. As the tower died around them, the Drowned Priest tried to bar their escape with a wall of faithful pilgrims, but Petra's words and Anselm's cold truth broke his following while Yarrow held the collapsing nave alone against both stone and a promise made in anger. They fled into the rain with Tomas alive in Caddock's arms, leaving the Hive Mother silenced and Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple swallowed by the flood behind them.
